title: Pity Him for a Night Whose End Drags On
intro: Al-Buhturi praises Yusuf ibn Muhammad, the Abbasid governor of Armenia, on the capture of Bagrat son of Ashot. In his account of 237 AH (851–852 CE), al-Tabari says Bagrat came to seek office and Yusuf sent him in chains to the caliph. The governor first enters the poem almost in passing, as the model for a rain cloud over an abandoned camp. When he reappears, the lover’s night gives way to a victor’s account of the capture and finally to the ranks before whom the poet performs.

translation: Pity him for a night whose end drags on,
and for a clan about to leave, its camels being haltered.
1.sharh: He experiences two speeds at once. The night will not finish, yet hands are already fitting the camels with the ropes that mean the camp is breaking up.

translation: If distance brings the tears down to water,
only the two camps drawing close can bring them back.
2.sharh: Camels go down to water and come away again. His tears have made the outward journey, and he knows of only one thing that could call them home.

translation: First home of theirs, at Darat Juljul,
may rain give you drink, its evening showers and early ones.
3.sharh: An abandoned camp receives the greeting one might have given its inhabitants. Morning and evening showers could keep faith with the place even after the people have gone.

translation: May it come to you in Yusuf ibn Muhammad’s likeness,
its scented breath soaking you, its rain falling lavishly.
4.sharh: Usually a generous man is compared to rain. Here the cloud is asked to model itself on Yusuf, whose name enters a love passage without interrupting the prayer for water.

translation: Yet if your campsite wished, its traces could tell
the lovesick man where his Tumadir is.
5.sharh: The marks on the ground ought to know where their former occupant went. He treats their silence as a refusal, which allows him to go on appealing to them.

translation: I shall turn my reins and ask
its wild calves where its wild calves have settled.
6.sharh: The first calves are the young of the wild cattle at the deserted camp. The second time he says “calves” he means the women who lived there, whose eyes he remembers in the eyes of the animals before him.

translation: Youth has run its course, save for a phantom that visits me
bearing a coy beauty, dark-eyed, languid of gaze.
7.sharh: Youth can no longer come back in person. The dream image comes in its place, bringing a remembered manner of looking as well as the features of a face.

translation: It crosses the black of night from a slender one,
delicate at the waist, with black braids.
8.sharh: The visitor is a likeness that can travel while the beloved stays elsewhere. The black of the surrounding night answers the black of the hair it brings to mind.

translation: It recalls our old bond and a night
by the acacias of al-Jiz', when its night-talker slept.
9.sharh: The memory has a precise time, when even the person who normally stays up talking had fallen asleep. One welcome night can still be recovered from all the unwelcome ones.

translation: And a pledge on which we could only differ.
I cannot forget it. The other cannot remember.
10.sharh: The two lovers remain paired in the sentence while the verbs take them in opposite directions. He cannot stop remembering something the other has ceased to remember.

translation: I have seen Abu Ya'qub, and people are either sensible
and place their hopes in him, or misguided and fear him.
11.sharh: Yusuf's own name appeared briefly with the rain. His familiar name Abu Ya'qub brings him back at the centre, and the court poet ranks others by their relation to him.

translation: He is the ruler to whom faith and high endeavour look.
His piety is God’s, and glory claims the rest of him.
12.sharh: The praise amounts to an allocation of the whole man. Reverence answers to God, and all his remaining powers are spoken for by honour.

translation: His might is feared, his open hand looked for.
Rain cannot come second to him, nor the lion make a tenth.
13.sharh: Rain would ordinarily set the standard for giving and the lion for strength. Both now have to qualify against him, one for second place and one for a mere tenth of his power.

translation: Grave in every bearing, he springs to give
to us. He commands the east, yet bounty commands him.
14.sharh: The line break holds back who benefits from this sudden lightness of movement. A governor recognises one command over himself, the impulse to give.

translation: If some misfortune comes close to him,
he turns his eyes to his sword for counsel.
15.sharh: One glance replaces a council of advisers. The weapon is made to answer a question, so the poet can indicate the governor's decision without spelling it out.

translation: When champions fall silent in the thick of battle,
his roars rise above the noise of iron.
16.sharh: Men famed for courage lose their voices first. We then have to imagine a single voice carrying beyond the clash that has silenced them.

translation: When anger flares in the glance of his eyes,
you see the deaths of men consulting him.
17.sharh: The direction of consultation reverses. A man who just sought his sword's advice now appears to be consulted by the powers that take human lives.

translation: No glory for unbelief, says the poet, since his armies met
on the slope beneath the heights of Taron.
18.sharh: The religious classification belongs to the Abbasid panegyrist. The physical location, a slope below the Armenian highland, leads into the capture of a particular ruler.

translation: It was hardly an easy place to reach.
But the lion in the thicket gave up his lair.
19.sharh: The country retains its reputation for inaccessibility. To account for its loss the poet turns its ruler into a lion that has handed over its own cover.

translation: In Yusuf’s eyes, Bagrat son of Ashot
was hardly the first slave brought to ruin by his offences.
20.sharh: “Slave” is the victor’s language for someone he treats as a rebellious subject. By placing Bagrat among a series of alleged offenders the poet makes him a warning to survivors.

translation: For fifty years he had made trouble for Islam.
Neither fear checked him nor forbearance restrained him.
21.sharh: The fifty years are the duration claimed in the praise poem. It presents pressure and leniency as two policies already tried before its hero intervened.

translation: Yet when the two hosts met he could not bring
his hands together, or hold his gaze on the blades.
22.sharh: The armies can come together, his own hands cannot. Two small failures of bodily control stand in for the loss of his ability to command.

translation: He would take no refuge in Jurzan’s fastness,
nor settle by a mountain spur in Byzantine lands.
23.sharh: The poet maps an escape route in the negative. Each named shelter the man declines makes his actual destination seem more startling.

translation: He came like a wild ass led by bewilderment
to a wide-jawed beast whose claws run with blood.
24.sharh: The former lion of his own thicket has changed animals. The new lion need not be named once the poet has let us see its jaws and claws.

translation: Whoever might blame him for surrendering,
I, for all that happened, find him an excuse.
25.sharh: Mercy appears to interrupt a victor’s account. His excuse will turn out to be another compliment to Yusuf, since escaping such a man was never a realistic choice.

translation: How could he elude a lion a mere glance away,
who had him under siege from two months’ journey off?
26.sharh: The two months measure distance in travel time. The governor had already exercised the reach of a besieger while he was that far away.

translation: Iron took his body in its weight. Firmly wrought
were the anklets and bracelets fashioned from it.
27.sharh: A craftsman's vocabulary gives the fetters a bitter finish. The ankles and wrists are indeed ornamented, but iron weight has taken the place of precious metal.

translation: If death should catch him in Iraq,
the caliph must count his captor as his killer.
28.sharh: The conditional matters. This is a claim for the captor's share of the credit should the prisoner die in Iraq, not a report that he was executed.

translation: Through your fortunate planning his own plot closed
around him, and his brown lances and cutting blades grew blunt.
29.sharh: Yusuf now receives the praise in the second person. His adversary's scheme becomes his own confinement, where neither reach of lance nor edge of sword can help.

translation: You folded away a secret so deep that, if it tried
to hide it from us, night’s own heart could not contain it.
30.sharh: Night is normally the natural ally of concealment. Given an inward mind of its own, it would still be a poorer keeper of the plan than Yusuf.

translation: No lord in Arran with an offence like his remains
whose wits have not deserted him and flown.
31.sharh: News of one capture travels farther than the army. For a ruler conscious of the same exposure, its first effect is imagined as the flight of his own wits.

translation: After him you shattered them as glass is shattered.
Who can mend the crack your hand has made?
32.sharh: A broken bone can be set. The question invites that usual act of repair, but the material he has just chosen is shattered glass.

translation: If this is only the first breach in their power
and you are now their neighbour, it will not be the last.
33.sharh: The geography does the work of the prediction. Having a new neighbour sounds almost domestic until one recalls what this particular neighbour has already achieved.

translation: Nor is the frontier Muslim who defies his Lord
far from the cup its unbeliever drained dry.
34.sharh: Religious affiliation grants no automatic exemption in this warning about obedience. The drained cup makes a past punishment the measure of one still to come.

translation: The rebel knows, however far away
his dwelling may be, that you will come visiting.
35.sharh: “Visit” is the ordinary word for calling on someone at home. In a rebel's expectation of this governor its courtesy takes on a chilling precision.

translation: A sword, a will like a sword, and an army
of stout strands, its cords twisted tight.
36.sharh: The implements summoned by the promised visit emerge one by one. Sharpness describes the commander’s will, whereas cohesion is the quality that matters in the host.

translation: It carries little in surplus supplies, save neighing steeds
held back as remounts, or steel it wears in layers.
37.sharh: Even “surplus provisions” turn out to be fighting equipment. Fresh mounts and layered armour are the only extras in a picture of purposeful travel.

translation: When it spreads across the breadth of open ground, Madhhij
takes its right, the people of Qays its left.
38.sharh: The wide ground allows us to see a previously compact host divided into wings. Naming Qays prepares the shift from a view of the whole army to an address to one part of it.

translation: Its Sulaym men strike terror into fearsome hearts,
as do A'sur in their mail and Amir.
39.sharh: The names give substance to the Qays wing. Its standard of courage is the capacity to frighten people who themselves inspire fear.

translation: Men of Qays, Qays Aylan, you
guard the fray on battle day and feed its fire.
40.sharh: The second naming invokes a lineage, calling the listeners together as kin. Those who hold the line are also the ones who stoke the conflict.

translation: You hurried to the prince’s aid. He has always
befriended his allies, and his supporter finds support.
41.sharh: Their action establishes a claim within a continuing relationship. The repeated sounds of loyalty and aid make reciprocity audible.

translation: Great though the service you have done him is,
he will repay it with his gifts, and thank you for it.
42.sharh: A reward alone could look like the price of service. Gratitude gives the men a public acknowledgement alongside what the prince can bestow.

translation: He has become a fair division. His gifts go to you,
his distinctions to the noble line of Nabhan ibn Amr.
43.sharh: His allies receive the tangible proceeds, his forebears the distinction added to their name. The praise avoids making a competition between the two claims.

translation: Little wonder you face the spears before him.
His own clans have taken no tithe of his bounty from you.
44.sharh: His kinsmen might have claimed the first share of his largesse. Their failure to levy even a tenth on Qays gives the poet a numerical way of expressing loyalty bought by no family preference.

translation: If all you had were these deeds of yours,
enough to set his poet on his feet between the ranks.
45.sharh: The condition leaves its conclusion to the assembled audience. They can see the evidence standing between their two rows, the poet reciting these very lines.

1.2.1-2.head: وَشك نَوى
1.2.1-2.meaning: “Parting close at hand.” The clan has still to set out, yet he already feels the distance.

1.2.4-5.head: زَمَّ البَعير
1.2.4-5.meaning: “Its camels are being haltered.” Fitting the leading rope makes departure imminent.

2.1.3-4.head: وِرد الدَّمع
2.1.3-4.meaning: “The tears’ coming to water.” The term ordinarily describes livestock arriving to drink.

2.2.3.head: حِلّة
2.2.3.meaning: Two encampments, each including the people who have settled there.

2.2.4.head: مَصدَر
2.2.4.meaning: Ways back from the watering place, the return journey after drinking.

3.1.3-4.head: دارَة جُلجُل
3.1.3-4.meaning: Darat Juljul, a camping ground in Najd also remembered in the poetry of Imru' al-Qays.

3.2.2.head: حَيا
3.2.2.meaning: Life-giving rain. The prayer is for the place the beloved has left.

3.2.3-4.head: رَوحة وباكِرَة
3.2.3-4.meaning: Its evening and early showers, imagined as visitors who arrive at opposite ends of the day.

4.1.3-5.head: يوسُف بن مُحَمَّد
4.1.3-5.meaning: Yusuf ibn Muhammad, governor of Armenia under al-Mutawakkil. The poet introduces him here as the cloud’s model of generosity.

4.2.2.head: رَيّا
4.2.2.meaning: Sweet scent, here the fragrance of the rain as the cloud draws near.

5.1.5.head: رَبع
5.1.5.meaning: A former campsite, still legible from the marks its people left on the ground.

5.2.2.head: صَبّ
5.2.2.meaning: A lovesick man. The speaker refers to himself in the third person.

5.2.4.head: تُماضِر
5.2.4.meaning: Tumadir, the beloved in the opening. The possessive ending makes her “his Tumadir”.

6.1.2-4.head: ثَنى العِنان
6.1.2-4.meaning: “Turning my reins.” Changing the horse’s course lets the lover stop to make his enquiry.

6.2.2-4.head: جُؤذَر
6.2.2-4.meaning: A wild cow’s calf. He asks the young animals where the other “calves”, the women whose eyes resemble theirs, have gone.

7.2.4-5.head: أَحوَر الطَّرف
7.2.4-5.meaning: An eye with a striking contrast between its dark centre and bright white.

8.2.5.head: غَديرَة
8.2.5.meaning: Braids or tresses, the second patch of black in this night scene.

9.2.2-3.head: سَمُرات الجِزع
9.2.2-3.meaning: The acacias at al-Jiz', a valley bend or locality. Their remembered shade pinpoints the encounter.

9.2.6.head: سامِر
9.2.6.meaning: An evening companion or night-talker, a person one might otherwise expect to be awake.

10.1.5.head: تَبايُن
10.1.5.meaning: Divergence. Each lover’s relation to the old promise is the reverse of the other’s.

11.1.2-3.head: أَبو يَعقوب
11.1.2-3.meaning: Abu Ya'qub, Yusuf’s familiar name. It marks his return as the subject of praise.

11.1.6.meaning: Sound judgement or good sense, here displayed by the person who looks to Yusuf for help.

12.1.5.head: عُلا
12.1.5.meaning: Eminence, the heights to which a person’s honour and public standing can rise.

13.2.6.head: عاشِر
13.2.6.meaning: One who takes or reaches a tenth. Even the lion cannot match a tenth of his courage.

14.1.1-2.head: وَقور النَّواحي
14.1.1-2.meaning: “Grave in every aspect.” Generosity alone can make this composed man move in haste.

15.1.5.head: مُلِمّة
15.1.5.meaning: A calamity that descends on someone and demands a response.

15.2.4.head: حُسام
15.2.4.meaning: A keen-edged sword, here the counsellor to whom the prince turns.

16.1.5-6.head: حَمَس الوَغى
16.1.5-6.meaning: “The fury of the fray.” The old word for battle also carries the sound made by the combatants.

16.2.5.head: زَمجَرَة
16.2.5.meaning: Deep growls or roars, audible here over the noise of armour and blades.

17.2.5.head: آمَرَ
17.2.5.meaning: To consult someone. The agents of death wait upon the commander for counsel.

18.2.4-5.head: عُليا طَرون
18.2.4-5.meaning: Upper Taron, the Armenian district around Mush. The armies meet on a slope in its high country.

19.1.5.head: مَرام
19.1.5.meaning: The objective or object of an attempt, here the territory the army means to reach.

19.2.5.head: خادِر
19.2.5.meaning: The lion in its lair. Its departure leaves the thicket undefended.

20.1.3-5.head: بُقراط بن آشوط
20.1.3-5.meaning: Bagrat son of Ashot, Bagratuni prince of Taron. Al-Tabari calls him the chief of the patricians and records his removal in chains.

20.2.3-4.head: أَوبَقَتهُ جَرائِرُهُ
20.2.3-4.meaning: “His offences ruined him.” The description assigns guilt in the language of the victorious court.

21.1.5.head: حِجّة
21.1.5.meaning: A year, counted by the return of the annual pilgrimage.

22.2.5.head: بيض
22.2.5.meaning: Bright blades. Their gleam gives the swords their conventional colour name.

23.1.4.head: جُرزان
23.1.4.meaning: Jurzan, the medieval Arabic name for a district of eastern Georgia associated with Tbilisi.

23.2.5.head: رَيد
23.2.5.meaning: A mountain spur or projecting ridge, a possible place of refuge.

24.1.3.head: عَير
24.1.3.meaning: A wild ass. The change of animal reverses the picture of the captive as a lion in his lair.

24.2.2-3.head: أَهرَت الشِّدقَين
24.2.2-3.meaning: “Wide at both corners of the mouth.” The epithet supplies the lion’s jaws without naming the creature.

24.2.4.head: دَمِيَ
24.2.4.meaning: To run with blood. Al-Amidi quotes the line with the verb the reciter uses. Both diwan editions give «تندى», “grow moist”, leaving the liquid unnamed.

25.2.7.head: عاذِر
25.2.7.meaning: One who grants an excuse, here on the grounds that the captor could hardly have been escaped.

26.1.5-6.head: قيد لَحظَة
26.1.5-6.meaning: “An eye’s reach.” The distance a glance can travel, set against two months on the road.

27.2.1.head: خَلخال
27.2.1.meaning: Anklets. Iron fetters are given the name of jewellery worn above the feet.

27.2.3.head: صَوغ
27.2.3.meaning: Working metal into shape, especially the work of a jeweller.

28.2.4.head: آسِر
28.2.4.meaning: His captor, the man who takes him alive and is to receive credit even for a later death.

29.2.3-4.head: سُمر وبَواتِر
29.2.3-4.meaning: Brown-shafted lances and cleaving swords, two kinds of weapon rendered powerless together.

30.1.1-2.head: طَيّ السِّرّ
30.1.1-2.meaning: “Folding up a secret.” A plan can be tucked out of sight like the inner surface of a folded garment.

30.2.1.meaning: Deep night-darkness, endowed with a mind in which something might be concealed.

31.1.3.head: بِطريق
31.1.3.meaning: Batriq, a patrician or high-ranking commander. Arabic historians apply the title to Armenian princes as well.

31.2.1.head: أَرّان
31.2.1.meaning: Arran, a region of the southern Caucasus around the Kura and the Aras.

32.2.3.head: وَهى
32.2.3.meaning: A breach or crack, here a fracture in their power.

33.1.5.head: نَقص
33.1.5.meaning: Diminution of their power. The poet treats the first loss as a foretaste of further losses.

34.1.3.head: ثَغر
34.1.3.meaning: A frontier district, understood as a defended borderland and the people who live there.

34.2.5.meaning: To drain a cup to the last drop. The frontier ruler has had the full measure of punishment.

35.1.5-6.head: أَمعَنَ
35.1.5-6.meaning: To carry far away. The dwelling, named only in the next half, is what takes him into the distance.

36.1.4.head: جَحفَل
36.1.4.meaning: A great massed army, its strength now measured collectively.

36.2.3-4.head: مُحصَدات المَرائِر
36.2.3-4.meaning: “Its strands twisted tight.” Rope-making supplies an image of the army’s cohesion.

37.1.5.head: صَواهِل
37.1.5.meaning: Neighing animals, the horses identified by their sound.

37.2.1-2.head: ظَهارِيّ
37.2.1-2.meaning: Remounts held in reserve, ready when a fresh horse is needed in the fighting.

37.2.5.head: ظاهَرَ
37.2.5.meaning: To wear one coat of armour over another.

38.1.2.meaning: To spread out. The two editions and the reciter’s caption give this verb. The last consonant can sound like «انبتّ», “was cut off”. The next half describes the two wings of the army as it deploys.

38.1.6.head: مَذحِج
38.1.6.meaning: Madhhij, a large southern Arabian tribal grouping whose men occupy the right wing here.

38.2.4.head: مَيسَرَة
38.2.4.meaning: The left-hand divisions of the army, counted opposite the troops on the right.

39.1.4.head: سُلَيم
39.1.4.meaning: Sulaym, a branch of Qays Aylan. The possessive ending identifies its men within this army.

39.2.1.head: أَعصُر
39.2.1.meaning: A'sur, a Qays lineage named for A'sur ibn Sa'd.

39.2.3.head: سابِغَة
39.2.3.meaning: Full-length coats of mail, named for how completely they cover the wearers.

39.2.4.head: عامِر
39.2.4.meaning: Amir ibn Sa'sa'a, the Qays people completing this list of contingents.

40.1.3-4.head: قَيس عَيلان
40.1.3-4.meaning: Qays Aylan, a broad Mudar tribal grouping. Its warriors now become the poet’s listeners.

40.2.5.head: مِسعَر
40.2.5.meaning: Firebrands, and by extension warriors who kindle battle.

41.2.2.head: مَوالٍ
41.2.2.meaning: His allies or people joined to him by loyalty and protection.

42.2.2.meaning: One who repays a service, here with princely gifts.

43.1.5.head: نَوال
43.1.5.meaning: His largesse, the part of his distinction his allies actually receive.

43.2.2.head: سَرو
43.2.2.meaning: Nobility of character and standing, the inheritance to which these exploits add.

43.2.3-5.head: نَبهان بن عَمرٍو
43.2.3-5.meaning: Nabhan ibn Amr, traditional ancestor of a branch of Tayy to which both patron and poet belonged.

43.2.6.head: مَأثَرَة
43.2.6.meaning: Memorable deeds handed down in a family’s honour.

44.2.2.head: عَشَرَ
44.2.2.meaning: To exact a tenth from someone. His kinsmen have levied no such share on the other recipients of his bounty.

45.1.5.head: مَسعاة
45.1.5.meaning: Distinctions won by one’s own exertions, the deeds that give a praise poem its occasion.

45.2.4.head: سِماط
45.2.4.meaning: The two facing rows at an audience, with room for the reciter standing between them.
